name: Kanemizu iron-acetate tooth dye

card.summary: A traditional Japanese iron-acetate and tannin solution that stains teeth black, the dye behind the ohaguro beauty custom of dark, uniform teeth.
card.aka: Kane, kanemizu, ferric acetate dye, ohaguro dye
card.note: Historical custom; the dye is an iron-and-vinegar preparation and is not a modern dental product.

quick.overview:
Kanemizu is the dark brown solution of iron acetate, made by dissolving iron in vinegar, that Japanese women and some men used to dye their teeth black in the practice called ohaguro. Adding tannin from powdered galls or tea turned the stain black and made it water-resistant. Black teeth were considered beautiful and marked adulthood, marriage or rank.

The custom ran from around the 10th century to the late 19th century. Historians give several reasons for it: aesthetics, ritual, social status and a belief that the dye protected teeth. Today it survives in festivals, period films, kabuki and among apprentice geisha at a late stage of training.
quick.how: Historically the dye was brushed on with a feather or applicator, after teeth were rubbed with pomegranate peel to help it adhere. It faded quickly, so it was reapplied every day or every few days. Kabuki actors used a different mixture based on brown sugar and pine resin.
quick.risks: Historical accounts describe the dye as a sealant thought to help prevent decay, but modern controlled studies of it are not described. Iron acetate solutions are acidic and staining; Western visitors in the 19th century widely objected to the look. The practice was banned for men in Japan in 1870.

lead: Kanemizu (literally 'iron water') is a solution of iron acetate used to blacken teeth in ohaguro, the Japanese custom of dyeing teeth black. It was made by dissolving iron filings in vinegar to give a dark brown liquid; adding tannins from powdered Chinese sumac galls, or tea, turned it black and made it insoluble in water, the same chemistry as iron gall ink.[1]

In Japanese culture of the time, dark teeth were an aesthetic ideal and a social marker. The custom began among Heian-period aristocrats between the 9th and 11th centuries, spread to women of all classes, and in the Edo period was associated mainly with brides, courtesans and geisha. The government banned it for men in 1870, and it faded after Empress Shoken appeared in public with white teeth in 1873.[1]
No modern clinical trials of kanemizu are described; the evidence consists of historical and ethnographic accounts.

angle.text: The dye gave teeth a uniform black colour that was considered attractive and formal in its period. It appears in modern appearance culture as a historical reference and in ceremonial use by maiko.

paras: The base was a dark brown iron acetate solution. Tannin from gall powder or tea made the colour black and fixed it. A 1871 account by Bertram Freeman-Mitford in Tales of Old Japan describes a more elaborate recipe with wine, heated iron and gall-nut powder applied with a feather brush.[1] Before each application, teeth were rubbed with pomegranate peel to help adhesion, and the dye faded within days, so it was reapplied often.[1]
Kabuki actors used a separate preparation called hayagane, made with brown sugar and pine resin.[1]

The practice began among Heian aristocrats and appears in the 11th-century Tale of Genji. In the Kamakura period aristocrats and samurai typically began dyeing at their coming-of-age ceremony around age 15 or 16; later, girls started around 13 as a marker of puberty. In the Edo period it was limited among men to the imperial family and aristocracy, while among women it was mainly for brides, courtesans and geisha.[1]

Japan banned the custom for men in 1870, and the 1873 appearance of Empress Shoken with white teeth shifted fashion. It persisted among the middle and lower classes into the late Meiji period and nearly vanished after the Taisho period except among elderly rural women.[1]

Historians have not settled on one explanation. Suggestions include a cultural preference for black (as in lacquerware), contrast with the pale face powder and painted brows of the period, distinction of humans from demons shown with white fangs, a link between teeth and death, a symbol of loyalty among samurai, a dental sealant against decay, and a ritual marking adult responsibility. Sociologist Kyouji Watanabe argues it marked a girl's acceptance of adult responsibilities as a wife and mother.[1]
Nineteenth-century Western visitors widely criticised the custom; Rutherford Alcock considered it a disfigurement that discouraged women's attractiveness to others.[1]

Ohaguro survives in some festivals, period films, kabuki and some geisha districts. Apprentice geisha sometimes blacken their teeth at the final stage of training, and it features symbolically in the bridal sakko hairstyle.[1] Similar tooth-blackening existed in southern China and Southeast Asia, using different recipes.[1]
